trajectory_summary: The call opens with unusually high customer energy and curiosity, and the rep capitalizes on that by moving efficiently through bill collection and into a booked Saturday appointment. However, the rep never resolves a contradiction the customer himself introduces about home ownership, and lets a clear referral/neighbor cross-sell moment pass without securing next steps.
outcome_dispute: v1 tag is unknown; based on the transcript this is best read as a booked appointment (Saturday between two and five, later narrowed to 2:00) but a FRAGILE one given the unresolved ownership question — the person booked (customer) may not be the legal homeowner needed for the program.

observed_outcome.quote: Yes. I can have someone meet with you this Saturday at 02:00.
observed_outcome.reasoning: A specific day (Saturday) and time (2:00) are agreed for an in-person evaluation meeting, satisfying the booked definition, but the actual homeowners (customer's parents) are never confirmed as attending or even aware of the appointment.

bill_anchor_audit.reasoning: The rep captures a specific kWh usage figure but responds with a flat acknowledgment ('Okay. Okay.') and moves to a residency-length question rather than turning the number into savings-curiosity or emotional leverage against the utility.

primary_coaching_focus.quote: Yeah. So it's gonna be under my my mom and dad's name. I live here with them, so the the entire program will be under their name.
primary_coaching_focus.why: The customer gives three contradictory statements about who owns the home and who decides (parents' name at 02:03, bills under parents' name at 02:42, then 'technically it is my house' at 05:33). The rep books the appointment with only the customer confirmed, without the actual titleholders on record for the call — this is the single biggest risk to the appointment holding through the closer's qualification check.

key_moments.quote: Awesome. Yeah. Because I got me and my bunch of my neighbors, that were installed. We were gonna go with, you know, Aurora solar or something like that. But, apparently, they just filed bankruptcy.
key_moments.stewart_read: Customer discloses a prior competitive relationship (Freedom Pro, formerly considering Aurora) that collapsed due to bankruptcy. The rep acknowledges sympathetically but never probes what was previously quoted, what system size was discussed, or what the neighbors' experience was — competitive intel the closer could use.

key_moments.quote: the way the programs work is you need to be the homeowner, which I have you here as. Was there anyone else on the side of the home with you?
key_moments.stewart_read: The rep's own CRM/lead record apparently lists the customer as the homeowner, but this is about to be contradicted by the customer's next line. This is the root of the ownership confusion that persists through the rest of the call — the rep is working from a bad data assumption and never fully corrects course.

key_moments.quote: Yeah. So it's gonna be under my my mom and dad's name. I live here with them, so the the entire program will be under their name.
key_moments.stewart_read: This is not the standard spouse/adult-child-on-title protocol (which assumes the homeowner is on the call and a co-decider needs to join) — here it is inverted: the person on the call is NOT the homeowner, and the actual homeowners (parents) are not on the call at all. This is a schema gap Ion should clarify: does the setter book with a non-owner household member and let the closer sort ownership, or does the setter need the actual titleholder on the appointment before booking?

key_moments.quote: Yeah. So it's gonna be me making a decision. I mean, technically, it is my house. So that's why I'm the one that's the decision maker.
key_moments.stewart_read: The customer now reverses his own 02:03 statement, claiming ownership and sole decision authority. The rep says only 'Okay' and proceeds to booking without reconciling this with the earlier 'it's under my mom and dad's name' statement — a second, distinct touch on the same unresolved ownership question.
